hits.text: Construct validity of the PHQ-9 in university students in Colombia: A Rasch analysis approach Med. clín. soc. 2025;9:e521 e521 INTRODUCTION The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ -9) is a brief, easy-to-administer, and interprets a major depressive episode (MDE) screening instrument (1). Because of its brevity and good reliability and validity (1,2), the PHQ- 9 is one of the most widely used MDE screening instruments in clinical and non -clinical settings (3,4). Two recent systematic reviews have concluded that the PHQ -9 is the most reliable and accurate tool for MDE screening, so it is enjoying increasing acceptance in the scientific community every day (5-8). Overall, the PHQ-9 has demonstrated adequate psychometric properties in both general and medical populations (1,9,10), including university populations (11-16). The psychometric performance of the PHQ -9 has generally been evaluated using the classical test theory (CTT) framework, which focuses on the concepts of true score and measurement error (17). From the CTT perspective, the comparability of test scores has the limitation that scores are "test dependent" (18), implying that a low score may be due to a person's low ability or a difficult test (19,20). Based on an analysis of the articles included in the systematic reviews on the PHQ-9 published to date, approxi mately 800 articles evaluated the psychometric properties of the PHQ -9 using the CTT model (4,5,8,21-29). CTT -based techniques could provide inaccurate diagnoses and do not consider the heterogeneity in each specific item (30, 31). hits.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). hits.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 6 injury, and possibly suicide (Pedrelli el al., 2015). Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. Clinical Question In college-aged students (P), how does screening for depression with the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) (I) compared to current practice (C) affect early identification of depression (O)?
